title: Magnetic Fields & Forces
description: Flux density, field intensity and the forces and voltages they produce.

study.title: Flux and flux density
study.body: A magnetic field is pictured as **closed flux lines**, packed closely where the field is strong. The flux density $\mathbf{B}$ (tesla, T = Wb/m²) points along the lines. The flux $\phi$ (weber, Wb) through a surface adds up B over the area; for a uniform B perpendicular to an area $A$ it is just $BA$. If the same flux passes through all $N$ turns of a coil, the coil's **flux linkage** is $\lambda = N\phi$.

study.title: Field intensity and Ampère's law
study.body: Currents set up the field intensity $\mathbf{H}$ (A/m); the material then sets $B = \mu H$, with $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ Wb/(A·m) and $\mu_r = \mu/\mu_0$ (several thousand for transformer iron). Ampère's law: the line integral of H around a closed path equals the net current through it (currents linked to the path direction by the right-hand rule count as +). Around a long straight wire this gives $H = I/(2\pi r)$, so B falls off as $1/r$. The graph shows B for a 10 A wire in air.

study.title: Right-hand rules
study.body:
- **Straight wire:** thumb along the current, the fingers curl in the direction of B around the wire.
- **Coil:** fingers curl with the current in the turns, the thumb points along B inside the coil (that end acts as the N pole).
- **Force or cross product** $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$: fingers along $\mathbf{a}$, bend them toward $\mathbf{b}$; the thumb gives the result.
Flux lines leave a magnet at N and re-enter at S.

study.title: Forces on charges and wires
study.body: A charge moving through a field feels $\mathbf{f} = q\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{B}$, perpendicular to both $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. A wire is a stream of moving charges, so a straight wire of length $\ell$ carrying $i$ in a uniform field feels the force below, with $\theta$ the angle between wire and field. The force is largest when the wire is perpendicular to B and **zero** when it runs parallel to B.

study.title: Faraday's and Lenz's laws
study.body: A voltage is induced in a coil whenever its flux linkage **changes**, because the field changes or because the coil moves. A large but constant flux induces nothing. **Lenz's law** gives the polarity: the induced voltage would drive a current (through an external resistance) whose own field **opposes the change** in flux linkage. For a sinusoidal flux $\phi = \Phi_m\sin\omega t$ the induced rms voltage is $E_{rms} = \omega N\Phi_m/\sqrt2 = 4.44\,fN\Phi_m$.

study.title: Moving conductors: e = Bℓu
study.body: A straight conductor of length $\ell$ moving at speed $u$ through a uniform field, with B, $\ell$ and $u$ mutually perpendicular, cuts flux lines and has $e = B\ell u$ induced across it. With a resistance $R$ across the rails a current $i = B\ell u/R$ flows, and the field pushes back on it with $f = i\ell B$, **opposing** the motion: this is how a generator converts mechanical power $fu$ into electrical power $ei$.

steps.title: Flux density and flux
steps.body: Magnetic fields are drawn as closed flux lines. The **flux density** $B$, in tesla (T = Wb/m²), says how densely they are packed. The **flux** $\phi$, in weber (Wb), counts how many pass through a surface. For a uniform B perpendicular to an area $A$:

steps.prompt: A uniform field of {{B}} T passes perpendicularly through a rectangular area of {{a*100}} cm × {{b*100}} cm. Find the flux $\phi$ through it.
steps.explanation: Convert to metres first: $A$ = {{a}} m × {{b}} m = {{a*b}} m². Then $\phi = BA$ = {{B}} T × {{a*b}} m² = {{B*a*b|Wb}}.

steps.prompt: Match each quantity to its SI unit
steps.explanation: $\phi$ is in webers, so $B = \phi/A$ is in Wb/m² = T. $H$ comes from currents per length (A/m), and $\mu = B/H$ has units (Wb/m²)/(A/m) = Wb/(A·m). $\lambda = N\phi$ is in weber-turns.

steps.title: Ampère's law around a wire
steps.body: Currents create the **field intensity** $H$ (A/m). Ampère's law says that $H$ integrated around a closed path equals the current enclosed. For a circle of radius $r$ around a long straight wire, $H$ is constant along the circle, so $H\cdot2\pi r = I$. In air $B = \mu_0H$ with $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ Wb/(A·m).

steps.prompt: A long straight wire in air carries {{I}} A. Find the flux density $B$ at a distance of {{r*100}} cm from the wire.

steps.title: Right-hand rule
steps.body:
Grip the wire with your right hand, **thumb along the current**: your fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field around it.
For a coil it works the other way round: **fingers along the current** in the turns, and the thumb points along B inside the coil.

steps.prompt: A long straight wire lies in the plane of the page and carries current from left to right. What is the direction of $\mathbf{B}$ at a point just above the wire (toward the top of the page)?
options: Toward the top of the page
To the right, along the current
steps.explanation: Thumb to the right: the fingers curl around the wire, coming **out of the page** above it and going into the page below it. B always circles the wire, so it can never point along the current or straight away from the wire.

steps.title: Force on a current
steps.body: Moving charges in a field feel a force, so a current-carrying wire does too. For a straight wire of length $\ell$ at angle $\theta$ to a uniform field the force is perpendicular to both the wire and B. Its direction follows $\boldsymbol{\ell}\times\mathbf{B}$, with $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ pointing along the current.

steps.prompt: A straight wire of length {{l*100}} cm carries {{i}} A in a uniform field of {{B}} T. The wire makes an angle of {{th}}° with the field. Find the magnitude of the force on the wire.
steps.explanation: $f = i\ell B\sin\theta$ = {{i}} A × {{l}} m × {{B}} T × sin {{th}}° = {{i*l*B}} × {{sin(rad(th))}} = {{i*l*B*sin(rad(th))|N}}.

steps.prompt: A current-carrying wire that runs parallel to the magnetic field lines experiences the largest possible force.
steps.explanation: False. $f = i\ell B\sin\theta$ and $\theta = 0$ for a wire parallel to B, so the force is **zero**. The force is largest when the wire is perpendicular to the field ($\sin 90° = 1$).

steps.prompt: A square coil of {{N}} turns with sides of {{a*100}} cm lies perpendicular to a uniform field. The flux density falls at a constant rate from {{B1}} T to {{B2}} T in {{dt|s}}. Find the magnitude of the voltage induced in the coil.
steps.explanation:
$A = a^2$ = {{a^2}} m². The flux changes by $\Delta\phi = A\,\Delta B$ = {{a^2}} × {{B1-B2}} = {{a^2*(B1-B2)|Wb}}.
$|e| = N\frac{\Delta\phi}{\Delta t}$ = {{N}} × {{a^2*(B1-B2)|Wb}} / {{dt|s}} = {{N*a^2*(B1-B2)/dt|V}}.

steps.prompt: A coil of {{N}} turns is wound tightly on an iron core of cross-section {{Acm}} cm². The flux density in the core is {{B}} T. Assuming every turn links all of the core flux, find the flux linkage $\lambda$ of the coil.
steps.explanation: $A$ = {{Acm}} cm² = {{Acm*1e-4}} m² (1 cm² = $10^{-4}$ m²). $\phi = BA$ = {{B*Acm*1e-4|Wb}}, so $\lambda = N\phi$ = {{N}} × {{B*Acm*1e-4|Wb}} = {{N*B*Acm*1e-4|Wb}} (weber-turns).

steps.prompt: A conducting rod of length $\ell$ = {{l*100}} cm slides along two rails at $u$ = {{u}} m/s through a uniform field of {{B}} T directed into the page, as drawn. Find the voltage induced in the rod.
steps.explanation: B, the rod and its velocity are mutually perpendicular, so $e = B\ell u$ = {{B}} T × {{l}} m × {{u}} m/s = {{B*l*u|V}}. (Equivalently, the loop area $\ell x$ grows at the rate $\ell u$, so $d\lambda/dt = B\ell u$.)

steps.prompt: In the same set-up (B into the page, rod moving to the right, away from $R$), in which direction does the induced current flow through $R$?
options: Downward (from the top rail to the bottom rail)
Upward (from the bottom rail to the top rail)
No current flows, because B is constant
steps.explanation: The loop formed by $R$, the rails and the rod grows, so the flux **into** the page increases. By Lenz's law the current must make a field **out of** the page inside the loop: counter-clockwise, i.e. up through the rod, left along the top rail and **down through R**. Check with $q\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{B}$: right × into-page points up the page, pushing positive charge up the rod.

steps.prompt: One side of a motor coil consists of {{Nc}} conductors, each {{l*100}} cm long and carrying {{i}} A in the same direction, perpendicular to a uniform field of {{B}} T. Find the total force on this coil side.
steps.explanation: Each conductor feels $f = i\ell B$ = {{i}} × {{l}} × {{B}} = {{i*l*B|N}} (perpendicular, so $\sin\theta = 1$). The forces all point the same way, so they add: {{Nc}} × {{i*l*B|N}} = {{Nc*i*l*B|N}}. This is how the many turns of a motor winding build up torque.

steps.prompt: A straight wire of length {{l*100}} cm carrying {{i}} A makes an angle of {{th}}° with a uniform magnetic field. The measured force on it is {{F}} N. Find the flux density $B$.
steps.explanation: Solve $f = i\ell B\sin\theta$ for $B$: $B = \frac{f}{i\ell\sin\theta}$ = {{F}} / ({{i}} × {{l}} × {{sin(rad(th))}}) = {{F/(i*l*sin(rad(th)))|T}}.

steps.prompt: A uniform field passes through a single wire loop lying in the page. The field points **into** the page and is **decreasing**. Which way does the induced current circulate, as seen from the front?
options: No current: the field still points into the page
steps.explanation: Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the **change**. The into-page flux is shrinking, so the current tries to keep it up by making its own into-page field inside the loop. Fingers clockwise gives a thumb into the page: **clockwise**.

steps.prompt: A coil linking a very large but constant flux has a large voltage induced in it.
steps.explanation: False. Faraday's law $e = d\lambda/dt$ depends only on how fast the flux linkage **changes**. A constant flux, however large, induces no voltage.

steps.prompt: Find the magnetic field intensity $H$ at {{r*1000}} mm from a long straight wire carrying {{I}} A.
steps.explanation: Ampère's law on a circle of radius $r$: $H\cdot2\pi r = I$, so $H$ = {{I}} / (2π × {{r}} m) = {{I/(2*pi*r)}} A/m. Note that $H$ does not depend on the material; $B = \mu H$ does.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the flux $\phi(t)$ in the core of a {{N}}-turn coil. Find the magnitude of the induced voltage while the flux is **decreasing**.
steps.hint: $e = N\,d\phi/dt$: the slope of a straight segment is rise over run.
steps.explanation:
The flux falls from {{Pm|Wb}} to 0 between {{T2|s}} and {{T3|s}}, so $|d\phi/dt|$ = {{Pm|Wb}} / {{T3-T2|s}} = {{Pm/(T3-T2)}} Wb/s.
$|e| = N|d\phi/dt|$ = {{N}} × {{Pm/(T3-T2)}} = {{N*Pm/(T3-T2)|V}}. (While the flux is constant, $e = 0$; while it rises, $e$ = {{N*Pm/T1|V}} with the opposite polarity.)

steps.prompt: The flux linking a coil is $\phi(t) = \Phi_m\sin\omega t$ (top graph). Which graph shows the induced voltage $e = N\,d\phi/dt$?
steps.explanation: $e = N\frac{d}{dt}\Phi_m\sin\omega t = \omega N\Phi_m\cos\omega t$: a cosine, leading the flux by 90°. The voltage is largest where the flux crosses zero (steepest slope) and zero where the flux peaks (slope zero).

steps.prompt: The core flux of a {{N}}-turn coil is $\phi(t) = \Phi_m\sin(2\pi ft)$ with $\Phi_m$ = {{Pm|Wb}} and $f$ = {{f}} Hz. Find the **rms** value of the induced voltage.
steps.explanation:
$e = N\frac{d\phi}{dt} = 2\pi fN\Phi_m\cos(2\pi ft)$, so the peak is $E_m = 2\pi fN\Phi_m$ = 2π × {{f}} × {{N}} × {{Pm}} = {{2*pi*f*N*Pm|V}}.
$E_{rms} = E_m/\sqrt2 = 4.44\,fN\Phi_m$ = {{2*pi*f*N*Pm/sqrt(2)|V}}.

steps.prompt: The rod (length {{l*100}} cm) slides at a constant {{u}} m/s through {{B}} T. The rails and rod have negligible resistance and there is no friction.

ask.prompt: Find the force needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed.
ask.explanation: $i = B\ell u/R$ = {{B*l*u/R|A}}. The field pushes on this current with $f = i\ell B$ = {{B*l*u/R}} × {{l}} × {{B}} = {{B^2*l^2*u/R|N}}, opposing the motion (Lenz). At constant speed the applied force must balance it: $f = B^2\ell^2u/R$.

ask.prompt: Find the mechanical power needed to keep the rod moving.
ask.explanation: $p = fu = \frac{B^2\ell^2u^2}{R}$ = {{(B*l*u)^2/R|W}}. Check: the electrical power in $R$ is $e^2/R$ = ({{B*l*u|V}})² / {{R|Ω}} = the same value. All the mechanical work becomes heat in $R$.

steps.prompt: Two long parallel wires in air, {{d*100}} cm apart, carry {{I1}} A and {{I2}} A. Find the magnitude of the force **per metre of length** on each wire.
steps.explanation: Wire 1 creates $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0I_1}{2\pi d}$ = {{2e-7*I1/d|T}} at wire 2, perpendicular to it. Force per metre on wire 2: $f/\ell = I_2B_1 = \frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$ = {{I2}} A × {{2e-7*I1/d|T}} = {{2e-7*I1*I2/d|N}}/m. By Newton's third law wire 1 feels the same force.

steps.prompt: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the **same** direction. What do they do?
steps.explanation: Take both currents out of the page with wire 2 to the right of wire 1. At wire 2, B from wire 1 points up the page (right-hand rule). $\boldsymbol{\ell}\times\mathbf{B}$ = (out of page) × (up) points **left**, toward wire 1. Like currents attract; opposite currents repel.

steps.prompt: A toroidal iron core ($\mu_r$ = {{mur}}) with a mean radius of {{r*100}} cm carries a uniform winding of {{N}} turns with {{i}} A. Using Ampère's law along the mean circle, find the flux density in the core.
steps.explanation:
The circle of radius $r$ is threaded $N$ times by the current: $H\cdot2\pi r = Ni$, so $H$ = {{N}} × {{i}} / (2π × {{r}}) = {{H}} A/m.
$B = \mu_r\mu_0H$ = {{mur}} × 4π×$10^{-7}$ × {{H}} = {{Bc|T}}. The iron multiplies the field of the same current by {{mur}}.
